sections.title: The Gate Between Networks
sections.body: A switch moves traffic INSIDE your LAN. A router moves traffic BETWEEN networks — it is the exit door of your LAN toward the Internet or other offices. Your home Wi-Fi box is actually a router (plus switch + more in one).

sections.title: How It Decides Where to Send
sections.body: A router works like a car GPS: it checks its routing table and picks the best road for each packet. Routes come from three places:
points: Connected routes — networks plugged directly into the router.
Static routes — a human typed them by hand.
Dynamic protocols (OSPF, EIGRP) — routers tell each other automatically.
sections.code:
Routing table example
-------------------------------
10.1.0.0/16  ->  GigabitEthernet0/0   (direct)
0.0.0.0/0    ->  203.0.113.1          (default route = "everything else")

sections.title: Broadcasts Stop Here
sections.body: A broadcast says "ATTENTION EVERYONE!" inside one network. Routers never forward broadcasts to the next network — they act as sound-proof walls. That keeps big networks calm, which is why large networks are split into subnets joined by routers.

sections.title: Switch vs Router
sections.tip: 💡 Exam tip: "Which device separates broadcast domains?" → Router. "Which device creates many collision domains?" → Switch (one per port).
